Special Commission of Inquiry
into Healthcare Funding
Before: The Commissioner,
Mr Richard Beasley SC
At Level 2, 121 Macquarie Street,
Sydney, New South Wales
Thursday, 18 April 2024 at 10.00am
(Day 019)
Mr Ed Muston SC (Senior Counsel Assisting)
Mr Ross Glover (Counsel Assisting)
Dr Tamsin Waterhouse (Counsel Assisting)
Mr Ian Fraser (Counsel Assisting)
Mr Dan Fuller (Counsel Assisting)
Also present:
Mr Richard Cheney with Mr Hilbert Chiu for NSW Health

THE COMMISSIONER: Morning, everybody.
MR MUSTON: Morning. Today we're having a day dealing
with or examining some of the affiliated health
organisations. Mr Fraser will be taking evidence from
witnesses who, as you will have seen from the line-up, are
Grainne O'Loughlin, Robert Mills and Matthew Mackay.
Ms O'Loughlin is the first of them, so without further
adieu, we will call her.
<GRAINNE ANNE FAITH O'LOUGHLIN, sworn: [10am]
<EXAMINATION BY MR FRASER:
MR FRASER: Q. Would you give your full name, please?
A. Yes. My name is Grainne Anne Faith O'Loughlin.
Q. You are the CEO of Karitane; is that correct?
A. That's correct.
Q. Ms O'Loughlin, how long have you been the CEO of
Karitane?
A. Coming up on 10 years, actually, so I joined in 2014.
Q. And Karitane, could you give a brief overview of what
it does?
A. Yes, sure. So Karitane is an organisation that
supports parents in the early years or the first 2,000
days, a statewide service, yes, supporting parents who have
new babies up to the age of 5.
Q. How long has Karitane been providing such services?
A. We were pleased to celebrate our centenary year last
year. So we're in our 101st year.
Q. It is correct, isn't it, that Karitane is recognised
within the Health Services Act as an affiliated health
organisation; is that correct?
A. Yes, that's correct.
Q. And those organisations, including Karitane, are
listed in schedule 3 of the Act; is that correct?
A. That's also correct.
Q. We will come back to that in a moment. Just in
relation to yourself, Ms O'Loughlin, prior to becoming the
CEO of Karitane, what was your general history in the area?

A. So I've worked in the New South Wales public health
service for 33 years. I'm a speech pathologist by clinical
background. I have been a director of allied health and
a senior executive in a number of the public tertiary
hospitals in New South Wales.
Q. In terms of those affiliated health organisations, we
understand that there is a body that represents them
collectively. Is that the Health Services Association?
A. Yes, the Health Services Association NSW, yes.
Q. Often referred to in shorthand as the HSA; is that
correct?
A. That's correct.
Q. Do you hold any position on the HSA currently?
A. Yes, I'm a current board director on the HSA and I'm
also the immediate past president.
Q. Your term as president of the HSA, what years did that
cover?
A. For the last five years, and I recently handed that
role over in November 2023.
Q. 2018 to November 2023?
A. Yes, that's right.
Q. Moving back to Karitane, it is a company limited by
guarantee; is that correct?
A. Yes, that's correct.
Q. Is it board governed?
A. Yes, we have an independent board of directors, yes.
Q. Does it have some status in relation to charities?
A. Yes. So we're recognised by the ACNC as a fully
deductible gift recipient charity. Yes.
Q. Just to get a little bit more detail in relation to
the services that Karitane offers, before we go into
locations and specific services, if we could just deal with
the types of service that it currently provides.
A. Yes, sure. So child and family health nursing,
parenting support services, as I said, for children, or
parents of children aged nought to 5. Generally, secondary
and tertiary, so we are not a frontline, we are
a specialised service, and we also offer perinatal infant

and child mental health services, including toddler
behaviour clinics for children with disruptive behaviours
and perinatal anxiety and depression, services for new
parents adjusting to parenthood that may experience anxiety
or depression.
Q. Generally, how would a family or parents or child be
referred to your service?
A. So, over the years, it's really been GPs,
paediatricians, psychiatrists, psychologists, child and
family health services in the LHDs. More recently and
during COVID we've had a self-referral mechanism, so that,
you know, parents weren't experiencing any holdups or
barriers to accessing specialised care. We've got a
website online referral, we've got a care line and an
intake phone number where parents can ring and seek support
and advice.
THE COMMISSIONER: Q. When you said "not frontline but
generally secondary or tertiary", by "frontline" do you
mean paediatrics or something like that?
A. I will clarify. There are what are called universal
services, so child and family health nurses that are
employed by local health districts to provide, you know,
that first six weeks of support that is broadly available
to everyone. We would normally see parents or families who
are experiencing maybe an extra layer of complexity or an
extra layer of support needs that needs to come in through
a higher level of intensive support care.
MR FRASER: Q. In terms of the New South Wales public
health system, in terms of the services you provide, is
that under a number of different agreements?
A. Yes. There are a number of different agreements
relating to the health services that we provide. So the
main agreement is through a service level agreement, an
annual service level agreement with South Western Sydney
Local Health District, but we do have some other agreements
that have been administered directly from NSW Ministry of
Health in recent years, including virtual residential
parenting services and virtual home visiting services, and
we do have a side agreement with South Eastern Sydney Local
Health District for a, by us, philanthropically supported
service in Wolli Creek, in South Eastern Sydney.
Q. We will come to those in turn. Thank you for the
overview. We might take you to the current service

agreement and the services listed therein. Operator, if
you could take us to [SCI.0008.0169.0001] which is the
2023/2024 service agreement.
A. Yes.
Q. Just without taking you to it, executed quite
recently; is that right, Ms O'Loughlin?
A. It's not fully executed as yet, so there it has been
signed by Karitane and it's currently sitting with the
district.
THE COMMISSIONER: There is a letter of 5 April.
MR FRASER: There is, yes, Commissioner. We will come to
that letter a little later on.
Q. Operator, if we could go to page 17 of that document.
Starting on that page, we can see there that there are
services listed therein.
A. Yes.
Q. Starting at the top there, primary, secondary and
tertiary level child and family health services. Now, are
they - we have then some specific services listed.
A. Yes.
Q. If we can just run through those, on the right-hand
side "Tertiary level services (residential unit beds)
provided statewide across New South Wales primary and
secondary level services within other LGAs".
A. Yes.
Q. What LGAs or LHDs is that referring to?
A. So for the tertiary residential unit beds, those beds,
whilst situated in South West Sydney for Karitane, are
accessible for families from anywhere across the state,
equally accessible. So it could be a family from any LHD
across New South Wales that can come through to those beds.
Q. And where are those beds located?
A. They have just recently been relocated to Campbelltown
Hospital precinct. They were relocated - we had two sites,
one at Camden and one at Carramar, Fairfield, and those
were amalgamated and moved to the Campbelltown Hospital
site in 2023.
THE COMMISSIONER: Q. It may be that it is defined

somewhere, although I can't find it, but would you be able
to run me through what is a primary level child and family
health service, a secondary and a tertiary?
A. Yes, of course.
Q. Thanks.
A. So if you think of what we would call a stepped care
model, so there are parents who maybe need some very
light-touch supports and when they come through to our
services --
Q. What would "light touch" involve, is that like
settling the baby or getting it to asleep?
A. Yes, sleeping and settling, but by "light touch" I
mean they might be able to get enough information from
a webinar or an online or a brochure or a website or a
link. So they may be able to self-help and get enough
support and advice without actually coming into contact
with a child and family health nurse from the service.
Someone then who does come in might need something like
a couple of hours of support or a phone call and just talk
through particular moments, so we would count that as sort
of the front end of primary. If we talk to a family and we
have very --
Q. What sorts of things might they involve, is it
nutrition or breastfeeding?
A. Yes, it might be some breastfeeding issues around flow
or pain or just getting into a routine or a rhythm or
a baby that won't attach or latch. It might be sleeping
concerns, so they can't get a child aged nought to five
into a sleeping routine. It might be toddler tantrums and
behavioural issues. It may be anxiety and depression
symptoms or sadness or having challenges - for either, you
know, parent or carer, so it can be mums or dads or carers.
So a whole range of issues that come through our front
doors.
Q. And then secondary is --
A. So secondary would be when a family have seen these
universal services and they have maybe got an identified
set of circumstances that require additional support, so
they might come to what we would call a day stay or
a parenting centre, still as an outpatient, but they might
come and spend three or four hours with a child and family
health nurse or see a psychologist or a social worker. And
they may come back for repeat visits to a space like that.

Q. Can you give me some example of what the issues might
be that would require that?
A. So if a person was having real challenges with
sleeping and settling, they might come and say they're
feeling - they might have a low mood and --
Q. Or exhaustion?
A. Or exhaustion, absolutely, and so fatigue. And so
both parents may be impacted and they are looking for,
I guess, advice, skills and support and education and to be
shown the way --
Q. Experience?
A. -- to navigate, yes, how to do it, especially a number
of first-time parents, just trying to adjust. But every
baby is different and we see families with, you know, two
or three siblings and all the way up to quite complex
needs, which might include domestic violence, child
protection issues, young parents, teenage parents, who are
very young or parenting alone, people with not much social
supports, new arrivals, refugees, trauma impacted, First
Nations families who may be experiencing some adjustment
issues, and a large volume of culturally and linguistically
diverse parents in some of the locations that we work. So
anywhere, when we say secondary and tertiary, it usually
relates to the intensity of support. So you might need
a psychiatrist, a paediatrician, a GP, psychologist and
social work for some families and others may only require
a couple of sessions with a child and family health nurse.
So we're trying to work out to meet that family where they
are at and what they might need in that point of time. It
may not be just a single point of the care, so because
we're nought to 5, families may see us when they have new
borns and they may come back to us nine months later when
they are having fussy eating with a small child or starting
solids and need a different set of advice. So all the way
up to transitioning to school.
I suppose most notably for Karitane, we do offer
a highly specialised service around children with
disruptive behaviours, so we get a large volume of
referrals for young children in that sort of two years
to --
Q. Disruptive at home or disruptive in day care or --
A. Disruptive everywhere, so preschools, disruptive at

home. This is, you know, beyond the toddler tantrums, this
is disrupting family dynamics and school and preschool and
day care situations, and so we've got specific evidence
based programs that we run for those children and they
would run from the child - well, earlier starting, now,
anywhere from 18 months to five years.
Q. Tertiary is inpatient, is it?
A. Yes, tertiary, we - well, we've also got the virtual
residential parenting service, which is the equivalent of
the inpatient physical beds, and that service recently
commenced, probably about three years ago now, through some
government funding, yes. But essentially, that's a
four-night/five-day stay, where you are in for quite
a while and seeing a multidisciplinary team of
psychiatrists and GPs and paediatricians and kind of that
24/7, day/night.
MR FRASER: Q. In terms of that tertiary inpatient
four-night/five-day stay that you have described. Is that
wholly provided at Campbelltown or is it also provided at
other sites?
A. It is wholly - for Karitane it's wholly provided --
Q. Yes, for Karitane.
A. Yes, so wholly provided by Karitane at Campbelltown.
The virtual residential parenting services, obviously our
staff are there, but it's statewide.
Q. Indeed. But if it is physical inpatient, it is --
A. Physical inpatient, it's just at Campbelltown.
Q. So there are, you said, 19 beds; is that correct?
A. Yes, we've got one unit with 19 rooms, family suites,
if you like, so not just 19 beds, yes.
Q. And in terms of the various disciplines of clinicians
that you just described, are they all staff that are
employed by Karitane?
A. Yes. So all employees - we do have some VMOs - so VMO
GPs and paediatricians particularly, so they have
a contract of employment with Karitane, yes.
Q. So they are either contracted to or employed by
Karitane?
A. That's correct.

Q. They are not NSW Health staff.
A. No. They are Karitane.
Q. I think you said that service recently relocated from
two sites at Camden and Carramar?
A. That's right. So we used to have eight rooms at the
Camden site and we had 11 rooms at the Carramar site, and
so we've really just combined the bed volume to
Campbelltown.
Q. In terms of the other services listed there, I will
just ask you, digital health services statewide - what are
those?
A. Yes. So well before COVID transformed all of us to
virtual health care, we developed a virtual home visiting
model of care, and that was instead of families having to
physically come to a Karitane site or a precinct for day
stay, they could have a virtual home visit, and that was
primarily to increase accessibility for staff who didn't
physically live close to a child and family secondary
service. So that one is primarily virtual home visits.
Also, the virtual residential parenting services are funded
by New South Wales Ministry of Health, and then as we have
emerged through COVID, many of our services, such as those
listed at Jade House, perinatal, infant and child mental
health services, have been able to be offered through
digital or virtual care modality and, again, that's helped
support accessibility for families.
THE COMMISSIONER: Q. That digital health service, it
says offered and it says statewide. That means it is any
LHD, is it?
A. Yes. So for the virtual home visits and the virtual
residential parenting service, they are statewide, yes.
MR FRASER: Q. In terms of funding --
A. Yes.
Q. -- those particular virtual residential service and
the virtual visiting service, are funded under separate
agreements; is that correct?
A. That's correct. So they are --
Q. With the ministry?
A. That's correct, yes.
Q. We will come to those in a moment.

A. Yes.
Q. The Randwick parenting centre - what is that?
A. So Randwick parenting centre is a secondary - one of
those day stay sort of units, it is located over in
Randwick. So historically, Karitane was an organisation
that was located in the eastern suburbs of Sydney. In the
mid 1990s we could see that there was, you know, families
were blossoming in the west and south west and there was an
agreement, prior to my time, for - with the Ministry of
Health, that Karitane's main services be located out to the
South West to meet the growing demand in south-western and
western Sydney. In doing so, it moved all the residential
beds down to Carramar at south west, but it retained
a secondary service for the south east Sydney families,
because it knew that those families still needed support,
and that has been retained.
Q. So that would provide some of those primary and
secondary services?
A. Yes, mainly the secondary services. So we would
have - we do have child and family health nurses located
there and psychology services. So that sort of - yes,
sleeping, settling, breastfeeding and mild to moderate
anxiety, depression, adjustment disorders, yes.
Q. I would like to ask you now about Jade House and the
statewide toddler clinic?
A. Yes.
Q. First of all, where is Jade House?
A. So Jade House is not an actual house; it is the name
of the service, and so it's a perinatal and infant mental
health service that is located at Carramar at the Fairfield
site, and we did develop - we realised that some families
couldn't travel all the way from Camden and the broader
LGAs to Carramar, so part of that team provides an outreach
service down at Campbelltown, same team, but they just
cover two sites, yes.
Q. And in terms of the service it is providing?
A. So again, it's sort of a medium-term, so up to nine to
12 months following the birth of your baby, you may have
symptoms of anxiety and depression; you may also have
pre-existing mental health issues. So it's primarily
a team of clinical psychologists and psychiatrists and it
would provide that slightly longer-term intervention. So

there is a number of services that are short-term or
Medicare funded, you know, 8 to 10 weeks of short-term
sessions. Our services are a psychotherapeutic service for
parents with moderate, you know, perinatal and infant
mental health issues.
Q. The last one listed there I would like to ask you
about, Oran Park?
A. Sorry, I just wanted to come back to you, I think you
did ask me about the toddler clinic as well.
Q. Yes, my apologies, the statewide toddler clinic?
A. Yes. So we do run a clinic for young children. We
are often receiving referrals from paediatricians and/or
psychiatrists or GPs or parents themselves with young
children with quite moderate to severe disruptive
behaviours, and so we run an evidence-based program called
parent-child interaction therapy. We are leading experts
in Australia in PCIT, which is the short term for that, and
we've got very highly trained staff who are able to go and
train other staff in this program, but we are a central
referral centre for PCIT care, yes.
Q. Physically, where is that provided from?
A. Again, it is primarily at Carramar at the Fairfield
site, but we do run an outreach service down to the
Campbelltown site as well, and virtually.
Q. And virtually?
A. Yes, so we can --
Q. And in those services that you do outreach to
Campbelltown, that's part of the same facility, is it?
A. That's right.
Q. As the 19 beds?
A. Yes. So on that site we have the 19 beds, we have
a small toddler clinic, we locate the virtual residential
parenting service staff there as well, and we have some
outreach staff from the Jade House perinatal infant child
mental health team and an educator and playroom support
coordinator.
Q. And this is all within the hospital campus?
A. It's on the hospital campus but it is a standalone
physical precinct.

Q. I will ask you now about the Oran Park integrated care
hub, presumably located at Oran Park?
A. It is.
Q. Could you explain what services that provides?
A. Yes. Sure. So Oran Park integrated care hub is part
of the Oran Park shopping town and there is a GP service
located within that shopping town and they have collocated
and brought in a number of other support service providers,
and so through an agreement with South West Sydney Local
Health District, and initially set up by a philanthropic
donation from the Perich brothers, Karitane provides child
and family health nursing services to Oran Park, and that
is a drop-in service or a referral book service, where
parents would come for two to three hours to undertake
sleep and settling support and feeding and get advice for
nought to 5, yes.
Q. Now, we've touched on the virtual - the two virtual
services.
A. Yes.
Q. Just in terms of the virtual residential service, how
does that work?
A. Yes, so up until COVID, we never provided any virtual
residential stay. I guess one of the core services that
Karitane would be identified for, in fact, is its
residential inpatient services. That's what most people
would recognise it as. When COVID came along, obviously,
there were staffing issues, there were risks to
unvaccinated babies, and we at that time sat down with the
clinical care team to see if we could redesign and recreate
the experience of coming in to a 24/7 residential stay,
into a virtual. So we did design a virtual residential
unit stay, and parents were virtually admitted on a Monday
morning, but they would be in their own home, and we had
child and family health nurses, GPs, paediatricians, the
whole team, still available and we would book - send
a package of care, but we would book video calls to that
family and have emails and phone calls throughout that week
from Monday to Friday and overnight.
So parents essentially had their child and family
health team on call to them, and we would schedule
appointments, admit them virtually, check in what their
needs were and what their goals were, and work on them
around the clock as much as they needed. So we ran that

for about 12 months as a virtual residential unit and we've
done some studies and published the outcomes of that.
But, then, in conversations with the Ministry of
Health, we recognised the value of this model of care, in
terms of access, and in fact, clinical outcomes, and there
was some New South Wales Government funding to set up
a virtual residential parenting service for New South Wales
on the basis of that, and there was four years' worth of
funding allocated for that from 2021 to - still going at
the moment, yes.
Q. Through to 2025; is that correct?
A. Yes, it's just had a 12-month extension, actually, so
it was due to - that funding tranche was due to end 30 June
2024, and there is an evaluation under way with the
university partners and so there is an extension of that
virtual residential parenting service at the moment
until June 30, 2025, yes.
Q. Is Karitane the only provider in relation to that
service?
A. No. Tresillian, who are our colleagues that provide
similar services across New South Wales - I think you will
hear from Mr Mills directly after myself. So there was
$10.5 million worth of funding allocated. There are
currently 20 virtual residential beds operating in
New South Wales, and that was a 50:50 split, so 10 virtual
beds to - I think it started at eight and then we realised
we had capacity to go to 10, so we both run 10 virtual beds
across the state.
Q. In terms of those clinicians providing the care, are
they based at Campbelltown? Are they the same clinicians
that are involved in your physical admissions?
A. Yes, so they were originally at Camden and Carramar,
so we had four virtual beds staff at Camden and four at
Carramar, but they do join that residential unit team, so
we have staff that are very experienced on the floor and
they rotate through shifts. So one week they might be on
virtual residential roster and another week they might be
on the place-based roster.
Q. I see. Different staff in a particular week, but the
same pool of staff being used?
A. That's right, with the same skills and expertise and
training, yes.

Q. And just in relation to the virtual visiting --
A. Yes.
Q. -- how does that work?
A. So virtual home visiting is basically that secondary,
so instead of coming to somewhere like Oran Park or
Randwick parenting centre for two or three hours, you can
have a virtual home visit in your own home to have that
sort of shorter intervention. So again, you can have
a video call or a phone call or emails and webinars and
packages of care, but you stay in your own home essentially
and it's like virtually having a child and family health
nurse visit you at home.
Q. And those staff that are providing that service, which
staff are they?
A. So they are the child and family health nurses that
are employed in the parenting centres, like Randwick and
Oran Park. They would interchangeably provide a virtual
home visit. There were two staff that were specifically
funded through the NSW Health contract, and so they -
that's all they do, they just do virtual home visits, and
they are located at the digital health service up at
Carramar, yes.
Q. So some of those staff providing that service are the
same staff providing --
A. Yes, it's sort --
Q. -- care in a physical sense.
A. -- of like a hybrid model of care, if you like. They
are very versatile, they have the same skill set and they
can offer a digital version of the home visit or - we don't
physically go out, Karitane does not go out to do home
visits across the state, so either parents come in to the
centre or we can see people virtually in the home, yes.
Q. And just lastly, you referred to a separate
collaboration, I think, with South Eastern Sydney Local
Health District, providing a service at Wolli Creek?
A. That's right.
Q. What's that service?
A. So there is an emerging evidence around what is called
integrated child and family hubs across Australia, and we
do a lot of work with the Commonwealth Government and

a group of people around integrated child and family hubs,
and that's where service providers come together to
provide, I guess, a whole suite of services to families
that neither of us can provide by ourselves. So we joined
the South East Sydney Local Health District service team,
and there is - in this hub, there is antenatal services,
where parents come and see their antenatal services, they
may see their universal child and family health nurse and
then they may see Karitane's child and family health
service and toddler treatment and we partner with NGOs and
social services providers so families can experience a more
holistic wrap-around level of support for social needs,
health needs, antenatal needs. It's sort of holding them
every step of the way but Karitane is not the sole provider
in that precinct.
I will say that that service is not provided as part
of our funding from NSW Health; it is a purely
philanthropically supported service that pays for that
child and family health nurse and associated costs. So
it's not - you won't see it in the service level agreement.
Q. So it is truly a collaboration, in effect?
A. Yes, it is a collaborative partnership.
Q. Each party contributing its own resource or resources?
A. Correct.
Q. And that brings me on to, just at a high level, are
there any other services that Karitane provides that are
not - of a similar nature that are not funded through
NSW Health?
A. Oh, yes. We have a number of services that are - so
you will see in some of our documentation that out of the
suite of services and funding that Karitane receives,
about - I think it is about 46 per cent of that comes
through the NSW Health, South West Sydney budget, but we do
receive funding from the Commonwealth Government to run
some national programs, perinatal mental health navigation
services in each state and territory, in partnership with
others.
We also are subcontracted by NGO providers and provide
services for organisations like Mission Australia, The
Benevolent Society, Barnardos and others, will subcontract
us to provide parenting support services in various parts
of New South Wales, and I guess we've got a number of

philanthropically supported services in Shellharbour and up
in Newcastle in these integrated care hubs that we're
working in partnerships with others in, but they are
philanthropically supported.
The other funding is Department of Communities and
Justice, so the NSW Department of Communities and Justice
funds Karitane to provide A significant volume of targeted
early intervention programs. I realise the technical
language, but this is families predominantly in the social
services sector with higher or complex care needs. It
might involve housing, you know, relationship issues,
parenting alone, parents sort of on that continuum of child
protection and keeping families safe. So we would run
supported play groups and connect with other service
providers for complex needs, and we also recently got
funded by DCJ as part of a consortium to run an integrated
young parent hub in Campbelltown, and that's specifically
for young parents in South West Sydney - there is an
overrepresentation of young parents in South West Sydney -
to help match them with a key person or a navigator that
helps them access all of the services that they might need
as a young parent.
Q. And those are provided or funded under agreements; is
that right?
A. Yes. So all New South Wales DCJ are funded through
absolutely a formal agreement, as with all the Commonwealth
contracts, there'd be Commonwealth agreements.
Q. We've referred earlier to schedule 3 of the Health
Services Act. I might just have that displayed. I don't
think we are displaying a bundle version but I'm sure
everyone is well and truly familiar with it. If we can
just zoom in in the middle of the page on "Karitane". So
the schedule lists particular establishments or services
that are recognised for the purposes of designation as an
affiliated health organisation, just by way of overview?
A. Yes.
Q. There are a number of services listed there:
Carramar, Fairfield, Liverpool and Randwick. There are
still a number of services provided at Carramar, I think?
A. That's right. So we've still got the perinatal,
infant and child mental health services of Jade House and
toddler clinic, digital health services intake, all our
corporate services, education, research teams, you know,

backbone staff, they are all still - and my team, the
executive team, are all located at Carramar, yes.
Q. And we've referred or discussed the Randwick parenting
centre.
A. We have, and it's still there in Randwick, yes.
Q. Fairfield and Liverpool?
